extracted: Table 3 is presented as published clinical cases involving hyponatraemia after phenethylamines. Editors' independent count of table rows: 52 rows from 1991–2018, 46 female and 6 male, ages 13–49 with one age unknown; 50 rows labelled MDMA, one methamphetamine and one ethcathinone with methylone; 21 outcomes labelled death, 27 recovery, 3 unknown and 1 blank. Sodium appears in 36 rows and is absent in 16: lowest per-row values range 101–130 mmol/L. One of those 36 rows has 137 on day one then 129 on day three, so all printed sodium values range 101–137. Ten fatal rows report sodium, 109–126, within the 101–130 range of 24 recovery rows with sodium. Amount is unknown or blank in 30 rows, including 14 of 21 fatal rows; numeric drug concentrations appear in 4 rows and other substances in 6. Ten fatal rows, including nine female rows, cite Rosenson 2007; these overlap the California cohort rather than form independent deaths. These are table counts, not verified unique patients or population rates.

Three fatal rows (Karlovsek 2005 twice; Libiseller 2005) have no numeric sodium or hyponatraemia among their effect labels. O'Connor 1999 has a blank outcome although its reference title reports a death; keep 21 labelled deaths and one blank, rather than assert 22 confirmed deaths. Salathe 2018 is labelled methamphetamine in the table although its reference title names ecstasy. These are internal discrepancies, not corrections verified from primary reports. Four quantitative concentration entries do not establish that all other cases lacked toxicological testing.

locator: Abstract (p. 1); Introduction continuation (p. 2); Table 3 (pp. 5–6); Sections 5 and 5.1 (p. 7); Sections 5.1.2–5.1.5 (p. 10).
extracted: As proposed by this narrative review, phenethylamine-associated hyponatraemia can involve serotonin-mediated ADH secretion with renal water retention, excessive drinking, and sodium loss in sweat. The review calls the relevant drinking accounts anecdotal and its oedema inference speculative, and says the mechanisms are not completely understood. It describes Henry 1998 volunteer ADH results second-hand; it did not itself measure these mechanisms or fluid intake. Its p.10 single-dose statement concerns most reported deaths or permanent neurological injuries in women aged 15–30, not most cases overall; Table 3 has unknown amounts in 14 of 21 fatal rows and cannot verify that statement.

extracted: The review prints 89% female and infers probable female predisposition from its case table. Editors' recount is 46/52=88.4615%, or 88.5% to one decimal; this differs from the printed 89%, with no alternate author denominator inferred. If two probable duplicate female rows are omitted, the conditional recount is 44/50=88.0%, not a verified distinct-patient sample. No number of female and male MDMA users is set against those selected cases, so these shares do not estimate susceptibility.

locator: Section 5.1.5 Gender susceptibility and hormonal influence, first paragraph.
extracted: Second-hand description in the review of Simmler 2011: randomized placebo-controlled crossover in 8 healthy men and 8 healthy women; plasma and urine osmolality, ADH and copeptin measured at baseline and after 125 mg MDMA (study condition). Copeptin, an ADH-secretion marker, rose in women but not men; no significant differences in ADH or plasma sodium are reported, but the review does not identify the statistical contrast. It does not specify a laboratory setting here; the primary study was not read.

extracted: The review reports that, once hyponatraemic encephalopathy develops, menstruant women were about 25 times as likely to die or have permanent brain injury as men or postmenopausal women (Ayus 1992). Other proposed hormonal and muscle-mass explanations are drawn from physiology/animal work rather than a test of those explanations in people taking MDMA; primary reports were not read.
